Are Full Rollouts Necessary for On-Policy Distillation?

Yaocheng Zhang ††thanks: Work done during an internship at Meituan. Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: School of Advanced Interdisciplinary Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: zhangyaocheng2023@ia.ac.cn    Jiajun Chai Affiliation: Meituan Email: yuanheng.zhu@ia.ac.cn    Yuqian Fu Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences    Songjun Tu Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences    Xiaohan Wang Affiliation: Meituan    Wei Lin Affiliation: Meituan    Guojun Yin Affiliation: Meituan    Qichao Zhang Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences    Yuanheng Zhu ††thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences    Dongbin Zhao Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: School of Advanced Interdisciplinary Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
Abstract

On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense teacher feedback along rollouts generated by the student and has emerged as a promising post-training paradigm for long-horizon reasoning. However, standard OPD typically generates full rollouts during training, which is computationally expensive and may expose the student to unreliable teacher feedback at late rollout positions, especially during early training. We identify the rollout horizon as a key bottleneck in OPD that substantially impacts training efficiency. Unlike Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), OPD does not require a complete trajectory or a final answer reward to provide learning signals. This observation suggests that full rollouts may not always be necessary for effective OPD. Motivated by this insight, we propose two simple horizon-control strategies: Progressive OPD (POPD), which gradually expands the rollout horizon during training, and Truncated OPD (TOPD), which permanently performs distillation on reliable truncated rollouts. Experiments on mathematical reasoning show that POPD improves the training efficiency of OPD by up to 3×\times, while TOPD matches OPD performance using only 10% of the rollout horizon, leading to substantial wall-clock and memory reductions. These results demonstrate that controlling the rollout horizon offers a simple and practical path to more efficient OPD.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical reasoning, code generation and question-answering (Shao et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). On-policy distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Yue et al., 2025; Lu and Lab, 2025), which optimizes models on rollouts generated by the model itself, has rapidly emerged as a core technique for LLM post-training. Compared with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on fixed demonstrations, on-policy learning exposes the model to its own prefix distribution and directly improves behaviors that arise during generation. Recent industry efforts, including Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), Thinking Machines Lab (Lu and Lab, 2025), MiMo (Team et al., 2026), and GLM-5 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), have incorporated OPD into their post-training pipelines, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-horizon reasoning.

Despite providing token-level supervision, OPD does not necessarily achieve high efficiency in long-horizon settings (Li et al., 2026). Standard OPD requires the student to generate a full rollout and then computes log-ratio signals between teacher and student over the generated rollout. This design introduces two inefficiencies. First, generating full rollouts is computationally expensive, requiring substantial decoding time, KV cache memory, and log-probability computation. Second, the supervision quality of late rollout positions may be noisy, expecially during early training. When the student policy differs substantially from the teacher policy, small deviations in early prefixes can accumulate over time, causing later tokens to drift away from regions where the teacher can provide reliable feedback. Therefore, teacher feedback at late positions may become noisy, biased, or even misleading (Li et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026). This problem is further amplified in sequence-level OPD, where the update for an early token depends on a return-to-go style accumulation of future log-ratio signals. Thus, unreliable signals from late positions can be propagated backward and corrupt the gradients assigned to early tokens. This analysis suggests that OPD in long-horizon tasks suffers not only from computational cost, but also from degraded teacher reliability and the accumulation of future noise.

A natural remedy is token-level OPD, which aligns each generated token only with teacher feedback at the same position. By shortening the log-ratio horizon, token-level OPD avoids directly propagating noisy future signals to gradients at earlier positions, unlike sequence-level OPD. However, this alone is insufficient for efficient long-horizon training. Token-level OPD still generates full rollouts and distills all positions from the beginning of training, causing the student to spend substantial computation on late tokens whose supervision may be unreliable, especially in the early training stage. This observation reveals rollout horizon as another important dimension of OPD design. Therefore, efficient OPD should follow two principles: using a shorter log-ratio horizon to avoid the accumulation of future noise, and prioritizing distillation from reliable rollout segments to avoid premature learning from unreliable feedback at late rollout positions.

Motivated by these principles, we propose two simple horizon-control strategies for efficient OPD (Fig. 2). The first is Progressive OPD (POPD), which starts training with a short rollout horizon and gradually expands the rollout horizon as training progresses. This curriculum allows the student to first align with the teacher on reliable prefixes before being exposed to longer reasoning trajectories. By avoiding noisy supervision on late rollout positions in the early stage, POPD improves training performance while reducing unnecessary generation cost. The second is Truncated OPD (TOPD), a simpler variant that permanently uses a truncated rollout horizon and distills only the reliable rollout segments. Unlike Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) (Shao et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025), token-level distillation does not require a complete rollout or wait for a final answer to provide learning signals. Therefore, even truncated rollout segments can provide meaningful supervision.

LLM reasoning experiments show that POPD improves the training efficiency of OPD and reaches strong performance with much less cumulative training time. TOPD further demonstrates that distilling from truncated but reliable rollout segments is sufficient to learn the teacher’s reasoning patterns, without requiring teacher feedback over complete rollouts. In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

  • ∘\circ

    We reveal rollout horizon control as a simple yet effective principle for efficient OPD, and propose POPD and TOPD to improve training efficiency while achieving stronger distillation performance.

  • ∘\circ

    We provide detailed experimental analyses showing that distilling only partial rollout segments is sufficient to learn the teacher’s reasoning patterns, and that earlier segments provide more effective supervision signals.

  • ∘\circ

    Extensive experiments show that POPD improves the training efficiency of OPD by up to 3×\times. Meanwhile, TOPD can recover the training gains of standard OPD using only 10% of the rollout horizon, reducing training time by up to 82% in our experiments.

2 Preliminaries

We consider on-policy distillation (OPD) for autoregressive language models. Given an input prompt xx, let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote the student policy and πg\pi^{\mathrm{g}} denote the teacher policy. The student generates a response y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) from πθ(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x). At each position tt, we define the log-ratio signal rtr_{t} and the student score function sts_{t} as

rt=log⁡πg​(yt∣y<t,x)πθ​(yt∣y<t,x),st=∇θ​log​πθ​(yt∣y<t,x).r_{t}=\log\frac{\pi^{\mathrm{g}}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x)}{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x)},\quad s_{t}=\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x). (1)

Here, rtr_{t} measures the difference between the teacher and student policies on the token generated by the student, while sts_{t} gives the gradient direction for increasing the probability of that token.

Sequence-Level OPD.

To align with the teacher response, the OPD gradient can be written as

∇θJOPD​(θ)=𝔼x,y∼πθ​[ℒ⁡(x,y)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(y∣x)],\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}J_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\Big[\mathcal{L}(x,y)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\Big], (2)

where ℒ⁡(x,y)=(log⁡πg​(y∣x)−log⁡πθ​(y∣x))\mathcal{L}(x,y)=\big(\log\pi^{\mathrm{g}}(y\mid x)-\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\big). Using the autoregressive factorization, we have

ℒ⁡(x,y)=∑k=1Trk,∇θ​log​πθ​(y∣x)=∑t=1Tst.\mathcal{L}(x,y)=\sum_{k=1}^{T}r_{k},\quad\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}s_{t}. (3)

Since past log-ratio terms rkr_{k} with k<tk<t do not depend on the current token yty_{t}, their expected contribution to sts_{t} is zero. Therefore, the sequence-level OPD gradient can be written as follows:

𝔼⁡[gseq]=𝔼x,y∼πθ​[∑t=1T(∑k=tTrk)​st].\mathbb{E}\left[g^{\mathrm{seq}}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x,\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\sum_{k=t}^{T}r_{k}\right)s_{t}\right]. (4)

Discounted OPD.

More generally, a discount factor γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1] can be applied to future OPD signals:

𝔼⁡[gγ]=𝔼x,y∼πθ​[∑t=1T(∑k=tTγk−t​rk)​st].\mathbb{E}\left[g^{\gamma}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x,\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\sum_{k=t}^{T}\gamma^{k-t}r_{k}\right)s_{t}\right]. (5)

When γ\gamma is close to 11, each token receives supervision from a long future horizon. This introduces future information, but it may also accumulate noisy or unreliable teacher signals from later positions.

Token-Level OPD.

Token-level OPD is the special case γ=0\gamma=0, where each token is only aligned with the teacher at the same position:

𝔼⁡[gtok]=𝔼x,y∼πθ​[∑t=1Trt​st].\mathbb{E}\left[g^{\mathrm{tok}}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x,\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}s_{t}\right]. (6)

This approximate optimization formulation avoids directly propagating future log-ratio signals to earlier tokens, which motivates our analysis of OPD.

3 Why Long-Horizon OPD Is Inefficient

3.1 Degraded Teacher Reliability

As shown in Fig. 4, to mimic teacher-student mismatch in LLM OPD, we use a 2D navigation task where the teacher and initial student are trained toward different targets. The angular difference between their targets controls the mismatch degree. Teacher feedback is reliable near its own high-probability trajectory region, but becomes increasingly noisy as states move farther away. This indicates that teacher reliability is state-dependent rather than uniform over the full rollout space.

3.2 Accumulation of Future Noise in Sequence-Level OPD

We next analyze why sequence-level OPD is inefficient under a mismatch between teacher and student policies. As shown in Eq. (4), the update at position tt depends on the accumulated future log-ratio signals from positions tt to TT. While such a return-to-go formulation can exploit future information, it makes early tokens sensitive to unreliable teacher signals that appear in later rollout position.

Fig. 3 illustrates this effect in the navigation task. When the mismatch between the teacher and student is small, student rollouts remain close to the trajectory distribution familiar to the teacher, and both token-level and sequence-level OPD provide effective guidance. However, under a larger mismatch, later rollout positions are more likely to enter regions where teacher feedback is noisy or biased. In this case, sequence-level OPD propagates these unreliable log-ratio signals back to earlier tokens during training, whereas token-level OPD effectively avoids this propagation of noise by only relying on the current log-ratio signal. We formalize this intuition with a simple noise model. The derivation is provided in Appendix C.

Proposition 1 (Accumulation of Future Noise)

Consider the sequence-level OPD advantage at position tt:

A^tseq=∑k=tTγk−t​rk,\hat{A}^{\mathrm{seq}}_{t}=\sum_{k=t}^{T}\gamma^{k-t}r_{k}, (7)

where rkr_{k} is the log-ratio signal at position kk. Suppose that rkr_{k} can be decomposed as

rk=rk⋆+σk​zk,zk∼𝒩⁡(0,1),r_{k}=r_{k}^{\star}+\sigma_{k}z_{k},\qquad z_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), (8)

where rk⋆r_{k}^{\star} is the ideal log-ratio signal and σk​zk\sigma_{k}z_{k} denotes stochastic noise. In particular, when γ=1\gamma=1 and the noise scale grows with the rollout position, e.g., σk=δ​k\sigma_{k}=\delta k, the mean-squared error of the sequence-level advantage satisfies

MSEt​(A^tseq−At⋆)=δ2​∑k=tTk2.\mathrm{MSE}_{t}\left(\hat{A}^{\mathrm{seq}}_{t}-A^{\star}_{t}\right)=\delta^{2}\sum_{k=t}^{T}k^{2}. (9)

Thus, earlier tokens accumulate more future noise, with error growing as O⁡(T3)O(T^{3}) when t=1t=1.

When the teacher is optimal, the noise term σk​zk\sigma_{k}z_{k} in Proposition 1 vanishes, so future log-ratio signals can still provide accurate guidance. Therefore, sequence-level OPD can successfully distill the teacher policy under an optimal teacher compared to a suboptimal teacher (Appendix E.1). However, in practical LLM post-training scenarios, the teacher policy is rarely optimal.

3.3 Design Principles

The above analysis suggests that efficient OPD should follow two design principles.

Principle 1: Use shorter log-ratio horizon.

Sequence-level OPD assigns each token a return-to-go style signal that accumulates future log-ratio terms between teacher and student. As shown in Proposition 1, this accumulation can introduce noise from unreliable future positions, thereby corrupting the gradients of early tokens. A natural way to avoid this issue is to use token-level OPD. As shown in Eq. (6), instead of assigning a cumulative future signal to each token, token-level OPD only aligns the student with the teacher feedback at the same position. This form prevents unreliable future log-ratio signals from being propagated to earlier tokens, thereby leading to more efficient training. For this reason, token-level OPD has become a common and practical choice in recent academic and industrial distillation settings (Lu and Lab, 2025; Team et al., 2026).

Principle 2: Control the rollout horizon.

A shorter log-ratio horizon alone is not sufficient for efficient OPD. Even with token-level OPD, standard OPD still generates and distills full rollouts from the beginning of training. Distilling tokens at these late positions can increase training cost while providing only limited or noisy learning signals (section 6.3). Therefore, OPD should avoid relying on full rollouts too early or when they are unnecessary. One strategy is to progressively expand the rollout horizon as the student becomes better aligned with the teacher. Another strategy is to permanently distill only truncated rollouts when partial rollout segments already provide sufficient supervision.

Together, these two principles motivate POPD and TOPD. We use token-level OPD to avoid noise accumulation, while controlling the rollout horizon to reduce unnecessary long-horizon generation.

4 Methods

4.1 Progressive On-Policy Distillation

In this section, we first introduce Progressive OPD (POPD), a simple horizon curriculum for improving the efficiency of OPD in long-horizon tasks. The key idea of POPD is to start distillation from short partial rollouts and gradually expand the rollout horizon as training progresses. This allows the student to first align with the teacher on reliable early prefixes, before being exposed to longer reasoning trajectories. Instead of using the full trajectory from the beginning, POPD only applies OPD to the first HkH_{k} positions at training step kk:

𝔼⁡[gpopd]=𝔼x,y∼πθ​[∑t=1Hkrt​st],\mathbb{E}\left[g_{\mathrm{popd}}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H_{k}}}r_{t}s_{t}\right], (10)

where HkH_{k} is the rollout horizon used at training step kk. We use a progressive schedule:

Hk=min⁡(T,H0+Δ​H​⌊kΔ​k⌋),H_{k}=\min\left(T,\,H_{0}+\Delta H\left\lfloor\frac{k}{\Delta k}\right\rfloor\right), (11)

where H0H_{0} is the initial rollout horizon, Δ​H\Delta H is the horizon increment, and Δ​k{\Delta k} is the interval for increasing the horizon. Here, ⌊⋅⌋\lfloor\cdot\rfloor denotes the floor operation. Thus, the rollout horizon remains short at the beginning of training and is gradually increased after every Δ​k{\Delta k} training steps. This schedule reduces exposure to unreliable feedback at late rollout positions during early training and lowers generation cost, since OPD can provide token-level supervision without waiting for the final answer.

4.2 Truncated On-Policy Distillation

As discussed in the previous section, a distinctive advantage of OPD over RLVR is that it does not require a complete trajectory to obtain the learning signal. Motivated by this observation, we consider another simple but effective variant, termed Truncated OPD (TOPD). Instead of generating a full rollout of length TT, TOPD only generates and distills the first HH tokens, where H<TH<T. The token-level OPD gradient can be written as:

𝔼⁡[gtopd]=𝔼x,y∼πθ​[∑t=1Hrt​st].\mathbb{E}\left[g_{\mathrm{topd}}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}H}}r_{t}s_{t}\right]. (12)

Compared with standard OPD, which uses all positions from 11 to TT, TOPD uses only the prefix of length HH. When H=ρ​TmaxH=\rho T_{\max}, where TmaxT_{\max} is the maximum response length and ρ<1\rho<1, the cost of the rollout and training stage is reduced approximately in proportion to ρ\rho, making long-horizon OPD substantially more affordable.

This truncation is particularly suitable for OPD in LLM reasoning, because the objective primarily aligns the student with the reasoning patterns of the teacher, rather than relying on the transfer of additional knowledge contained in the teacher model (Li et al., 2026). Therefore, even a truncated rollout can provide meaningful supervision for matching the reasoning patterns of the teacher.

5 Experiments

5.1 LLM Reasoning Experiments

Setup.

We use two student-teacher pairs in our LLM reasoning experiments. The first pair uses R1-Distill-1.5B (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) as the student and JustRL-R1-1.5B (He et al., 2025) as the teacher. The second pair uses OpenMath-1.5B (Du et al., 2025) as the student and JustRL-Nemotron-1.5B (He et al., 2025) as the teacher. All student models are trained for 2 epochs on the DAPO-Math-17K dataset (Yu et al., 2025) and evaluated on AMC23, AIME24, and AIME25 using avg@16. During evaluation, all models are allowed to generate full rollouts. We analyze and compare three OPD variants: OPD11 1 Unless otherwise specified, OPD refers to token-level OPD in the following experiments., TOPD, and POPD.

Progressive OPD improves training efficiency.

Fig. 5 compares the training dynamics of standard OPD and POPD on AIME24. POPD reaches strong performance much faster than standard OPD. This result supports our hypothesis that standard OPD is inefficient in long-horizon reasoning tasks. Early in training, generating and distilling complete trajectories can waste computation on late positions where teacher feedback may be less reliable. By first training on shorter rollouts and gradually expanding the horizon, POPD reduces unnecessary long-horizon generation while preserving useful token-level supervision.

Truncated OPD provides a trade-off between cost and performance.

Table  1 shows that moderate truncation matches or outperforms standard OPD while substantially reducing training time. For example, TOPD with ρ=25%\rho=25\% improves AIME24 accuracy from 49.3 to 51.3 and reduces training time from 29.7h to 10.2h. Even with ρ=10%\rho=10\%, TOPD retains most of the performance gain with only 5.3h of training. These results show that OPD can effectively benefit from partial rollouts during training, since token-level log-ratio feedback does not require a final answer.

5.2 Analysis on Autoregressive Control Task

Setup.

To further evaluate POPD in a broader range of task scenarios, we introduce an autoregressive 2D control task (see Appendix D). Compared with the simple navigation task in Sec 3.1, this environment requires the policy to make decisions based on historical velocity sequences, making the task more challenging.

As shown in Fig. 7. POPD achieves a high success rate much faster than standard OPD. This again supports our claim that full rollouts can be inefficient, especially during early training, because late rollout positions may already deviate from the distribution familiar to the teacher and provide less reliable supervision. By starting from truncated rollouts and progressively expanding the horizon, POPD avoids premature learning from noisy feedback signals and accelerates convergence.

6 Why Training on Truncated Rollouts Is Effective

6.1 Prefix-continuation Analysis

The previous results show that OPD does not necessarily require full rollouts to improve the student model. Even when distillation is applied only to truncated rollouts, the student can still recover a large fraction of the performance of the teacher. We next examine whether TOPD works merely because teacher-generated prefixes activate better sampling paths. To isolate this prefix effect from parameter updating, we conduct a prefix-continuation experiment without updating the student. The student is R1-Distill-1.5B, and the teacher is JustRL-R1-1.5B.

As shown in Fig. 8, continuing from teacher-generated prefixes with length ratio ρ\rho yields only modest improvement, far smaller than OPD training on ρ\rho-truncated rollouts. Therefore,

Moreover, after TOPD training, the student model achieves the same performance with or without teacher-generated prefixes, regardless of the length of those prefixes (see Fig. 9). This indicates that

In summary, TOPD is effective not because imitating teacher prefixes can activate particular successful sampling paths, but because applying distillation on truncated rollouts improves the student by updating model parameters with dense teacher feedback over partial rollouts.

6.2 Analysis of Reverse Distillation

To further test whether TOPD provides a strong optimization signal, we conduct a reverse distillation experiment. Here, the weaker R1-Distill-1.5B is used as the teacher, while the stronger JustRL-R1-1.5B is used as the student. If OPD on truncated rollouts is indeed effective, then even when the teacher is weaker, the student should be pulled toward the teacher’s behavior.

As shown in Fig. 10, reverse distillation decreases the performance of JustRL-R1-1.5B toward the level of R1-Distill-1.5B, even when training over truncated rollouts. This also confirms that on-policy distilling on truncated rollouts is strong enough to reshape the student policy, without full rollouts or final answer supervision. Together with the prefix-continuation analysis, this result supports our claim that TOPD works through genuine parameter updating. Truncated rollouts already contain sufficient information about the teacher’s reasoning patterns, including problem decomposition, intermediate setup, and initial solution direction. By aligning the student with these early rollout segments, OPD can efficiently transfer the teacher’s reasoning patterns to the student.

6.3 Where Does Useful Distillation Signal Come From?

To understand why TOPD can match or even outperform standard OPD, we conduct a segment-level distillation analysis. We split each rollout into several 10% segments, including 0–10%, 20–30%, …, and 80–90%, and distill the student using only one segment at a time while masking out the remaining tokens. This setup investigates whether arbitrary rollout segments can provide sufficient supervision for learning the teacher’s reasoning patterns.

As shown in Figure 11, early and middle rollout segments provide more effective supervision. Performance gradually declines when distillation is applied to later segments, and can even fall below the initial policy. This suggests that teacher feedback may becomes less reliable along the rollout (see Fig. 12), and late segments may introduce noisy or harmful signals. This explains why standard OPD may sometimes be suboptimal:

Overall, this analysis supports our key claim that full rollouts are not necessary for efficient OPD.

7 Conclusion

In this work, we study whether full rollouts are necessary for efficient OPD. We show that OPD can be inefficient because full rollouts are costly and teacher feedback on late positions may become unreliable. Motivated by this observation, we propose two simple horizon-control strategies: POPD, which gradually expands the rollout horizon, and TOPD, which performs distillation only on truncated rollouts. Experiments on LLM reasoning and autoregressive control tasks show that POPD improves training efficiency, while TOPD achieves a favorable trade-off between cost and performance. These results suggest that full rollouts are not always necessary for OPD, and that controlling the rollout horizon provides a simple and practical way to improve the efficiency of long-horizon policy learning.

Discussion.

Our findings also raise a broader question for RLVR, namely whether training on truncated rollouts segments can effectively unlock performance on longer rollouts. If early rollout segments already contain sufficient information about the reasoning patterns, then optimizing truncated rollouts may provide a cost-effective way to induce behaviors that generalize to longer-horizon reasoning. However, unlike full rollouts, truncated rollouts are typically incomplete and may not directly lead to a verifiable final answer, making their evaluation a central challenge for RLVR. Developing reliable credit assignment or proxy evaluation methods for such truncated rollouts may therefore be crucial for extending horizon-control ideas from OPD to RLVR. This perspective suggests that horizon control may be useful not only for OPD, but also for improving the efficiency of RLVR, where long-horizon rollouts are often expensive and noisy.

8 Limitations

This work focuses on two simple and broadly applicable horizon-control strategies to validate the effectiveness of controlling the rollout horizon. A natural next step is to develop adaptive horizon-control mechanisms. For example, the rollout horizon might be dynamically adjusted based on the KL divergence between teacher and student, student entropy, teacher confidence, or the variance of log-ratio signals, thereby further improving the training efficiency and supervision quality of OPD.

Appendix A Related Work

MiniLLM first formalized OPD for LLMs under a reverse KL objective optimized via policy gradient (Gu et al., 2024; Yue et al., 2025). Unlike offline distillation (Kim and Rush, 2016), which aligns the student with teacher outputs or logits on fixed traces, OPD trains on student-generated prefixes and therefore better matches the distribution encountered by the student during generation. This property helps mitigate the distribution mismatch in offline distillation and enables a student model to effectively absorb capabilities from one or multiple teacher models. As a result, OPD has become an attractive component in recent LLM post-training pipelines (Yang et al., 2025; Lu and Lab, 2025; Team et al., 2026; GLM-5-Team et al., 2026). Recent studies have further explored how OPD can be combined with RL (Yang et al., 2026), or extended to self-distillation (Penaloza et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), where a single model serves as its own teacher by conditioning on privileged information such as expert demonstration (Penaloza et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026), execution feedback (Hübotter et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), question construction path (Zhang et al., 2026), or other high-quality auxiliary signals. Despite this progress, the efficiency of OPD remains relatively underexplored. Existing efforts such as EffOPD (Cai et al., 2026) analyze efficient OPD from the perspective of parameter dynamics and optimization behavior. In contrast, our work studies OPD efficiency from the perspective of rollout horizon control. We show that full rollouts are not always necessary for effective OPD, and that prioritizing reliable rollout segments can substantially reduce training cost while preserving strong distillation performance. This direction is orthogonal to parameter dynamics based approaches.

Appendix B Implementation

For POPD, we use the progressive horizon schedule defined in Eq. (11), where Δ​H\Delta H denotes the horizon increment and KK denotes the interval for increasing the rollout horizon. In the LLM reasoning experiments, we set Δ​H=9\Delta H=9 and Δ​k=1{\Delta k}=1. For all training runs, we set the original maximum response length to 15K, following the RL training configuration of the teacher models, JustRL-R1-1.5B and JustRL-Nemotron-1.5B, on the DAPO-Math-17K dataset. In the autoregressive navigation task, we use a finer-grained schedule with Δ​H=1\Delta H=1 and Δ​k=1{\Delta k}=1. For both the simple navigation task and the autoregressive navigation task, the maximum rollout horizon is set to 150150. The remaining hyperparameters for the LLM reasoning experiments are reported in Table 2. The remaining parameters for the simple navigation task and the autoregressive navigation task are shown in Table 3 and Table 4, respectively.

Appendix C Derivation of Future-Noise Accumulation

C.1 Noise Accumulation

Let the ideal sequence-level advantage be

At⋆=∑k=tTγk−t​rk⋆,A^{\star}_{t}=\sum_{k=t}^{T}\gamma^{k-t}r_{k}^{\star}, (13)

where rk⋆r_{k}^{\star} denotes the ideal log-ratio signal, and we assume that the actual received OPD signal can be decomposed as

rk=rk⋆+σk​zk,zk∼𝒩⁡(0,1),r_{k}=r_{k}^{\star}+\sigma_{k}z_{k},\qquad z_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), (14)

where σk​zk\sigma_{k}z_{k} is a stochastic noise term. Then

A^tseq−At⋆\displaystyle\hat{A}^{\mathrm{seq}}_{t}-A^{\star}_{t} =∑k=tTγk−t​(rk−rk⋆)\displaystyle=\sum_{k=t}^{T}\gamma^{k-t}\left(r_{k}-r_{k}^{\star}\right) (15)
=∑k=tTγk−t​σk​zk.\displaystyle=\sum_{k=t}^{T}\gamma^{k-t}\sigma_{k}z_{k}. (16)

Assuming the noise variables {zk}k=tT\{z_{k}\}_{k=t}^{T} are independent, then the mean-squared error of the sequence-level advantage satisfies

MSEt​(A^tseq−At⋆)=∑k=tTγ2​(k−t)​σk2.\mathrm{MSE}_{t}\left(\hat{A}^{\mathrm{seq}}_{t}-A^{\star}_{t}\right)=\sum_{k=t}^{T}\gamma^{2(k-t)}\sigma_{k}^{2}. (17)

When γ=1\gamma=1 and the noise scale grows with the rollout position, e.g., σk=δ​k\sigma_{k}=\delta k, the mean-squared error becomes

MSEt​(A^tseq−At⋆)=δ2​∑k=tTk2.\mathrm{MSE}_{t}\left(\hat{A}^{\mathrm{seq}}_{t}-A^{\star}_{t}\right)=\delta^{2}\sum_{k=t}^{T}k^{2}. (18)

Using the square-sum formula,

∑k=tTk2=T⁡(T+1)​(2​T+1)−(t−1)​t​(2​t−1)6,\sum_{k=t}^{T}k^{2}=\frac{T(T+1)(2T+1)-(t-1)t(2t-1)}{6}, (19)

we obtain

MSEt\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}_{t} (A^tseq−At⋆)=\displaystyle\left(\hat{A}^{\mathrm{seq}}_{t}-A^{\star}_{t}\right)= (20)
δ2​T⁡(T+1)​(2​T+1)−(t−1)​t​(2​t−1)6.\displaystyle\delta^{2}\frac{T(T+1)(2T+1)-(t-1)t(2t-1)}{6}.

In particular, for the first token t=1t=1,

MSEt​(A^1seq−A1⋆)=δ2​T​(T+1)​(2​T+1)6=O⁡(δ2​T3).\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}_{t}\left(\hat{A}^{\mathrm{seq}}_{1}-A^{\star}_{1}\right)=\delta^{2}\frac{T(T+1)(2T+1)}{6}=O(\delta^{2}T^{3}). (21)

This shows that early-token gradients in sequence-level OPD can accumulate substantial future noise in long-horizon rollout.

Appendix D Autoregressive Navigation Task

We compare standard token-level OPD with POPD. As shown in Fig. 13, the initial student trajectory clearly deviates from the teacher trajectory, indicating a strong mismatch between the two policies. After distillation, both methods can guide the student toward the teacher trajectory, but POPD achieves faster convergence (Fig. 14).

Appendix E Further Analysis

E.1 Sequence-Level OPD Under Optimal Teacher Policy

Proposition 1 explains why sequence-level OPD is sensitive to long horizons. Even if the log-ratio signal at the current token is reliable, the sequence-level advantage may still be corrupted by noisy future signals. This explains the empirical observation in Fig. 3. Under a small policy mismatch, future signals remain useful and both token-level and sequence-level OPD variants work well. Under a large mismatch, the future signals become unreliable, and sequence-level OPD can be substantially worse than token-level OPD.

It is worth noting that this failure mode is largely mitigated when the teacher policy is optimal (Fig. 15). In this case, even if the initial student policy is substantially different from the teacher policy, the future log-ratio signals are still generated from an accurate policy rather than from an unreliable or biased teacher. Therefore, the accumulated future terms in sequence-level OPD can still provide a correct learning direction and guide the student toward the optimal policy. However, the return-to-go form of sequence-level OPD still aggregates multiple future log-ratio terms into the update of each early token. Therefore, although the systematic bias is removed, the variance introduced by the accumulation of log-ratio signals remains. This explains why sequence-level OPD can still learn an accurate policy under an optimal teacher, but its convergence may be slightly slower than token-level OPD, which relies only on the log-ratio of the current token and therefore avoids the variance induced by log-ratio accumulation.

E.2 More Analysis on Autoregressive Control Task

As shown in Fig. 16, we also evaluate an analytically optimal teacher setting under the autoregressive control task. POPD still improves training efficiency, but the gain is smaller than in the suboptimal teacher setting. This is expected, because an optimal teacher can provide reliable guidance even at late rollout positions. Overall, these results show that progressive horizon expansion improves the efficiency of long-horizon OPD, especially when the teacher policy is suboptimal.

Appendix F Memory Analysis of TOPD

We provide a simple memory analysis to clarify why TOPD reduces the GPU memory cost of OPD. Let PP denote the prompt length, TT denote the maximum response length used by standard OPD, and H=ρ​TH=\rho T denote the truncated rollout horizon used by TOPD. Standard OPD generates and distills the full response of length TT, while TOPD only generates and distills the first HH response tokens.

The peak memory consumption of OPD can be decomposed into two parts:

Mpeak=Mstatic+Mlen,M_{\mathrm{peak}}=M_{\mathrm{static}}+M_{\mathrm{len}}, (22)

where MstaticM_{\mathrm{static}} denotes length-independent memory, including model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states. This term is unchanged between OPD and TOPD. In contrast, MlenM_{\mathrm{len}} denotes length-dependent memory, including generation KV cache, log-probability buffers, and training activations. These terms scale with the effective sequence length.

For standard OPD, the sequence length is LOPD=P+TL_{\mathrm{OPD}}=P+T. For TOPD, the effective sequence length becomes LTOPD=P+H=P+ρ​TL_{\mathrm{TOPD}}=P+H=P+\rho T. Therefore, the ratio of length-dependent memory between TOPD and full OPD is approximately

MlenTOPDMlenOPD≈P+ρ​TP+T.\frac{M_{\mathrm{len}}^{\mathrm{TOPD}}}{M_{\mathrm{len}}^{\mathrm{OPD}}}\approx\frac{P+\rho T}{P+T}. (23)

If we only consider the response part, the ratio further simplifies to

HT=ρ.\frac{H}{T}=\rho. (24)

Thus, TOPD reduces the memory of response part approximately in proportion to the truncation ratio ρ\rho. In our LLM experiments, we use a maximum prompt length of P=1024P=1024 and a maximum response length of T=15360T=15360. The resulting effective sequence lengths and length-dependent memory ratios are summarized in Table 5.

Finally, the actual peak memory reduction is smaller than the ideal length-dependent reduction because the static memory term is unchanged:

MpeakTOPDMpeakOPD=Mstatic+c⁡(P+ρ​T)Mstatic+c⁡(P+T),\frac{M_{\mathrm{peak}}^{\mathrm{TOPD}}}{M_{\mathrm{peak}}^{\mathrm{OPD}}}=\frac{M_{\mathrm{static}}+c(P+\rho T)}{M_{\mathrm{static}}+c(P+T)}, (25)

where cc is a constant that summarizes the memory cost of per token. Eq. (25) shows that TOPD mainly reduces the length-dependent component of OPD memory, while memory MstaticM_{\mathrm{static}} remains the same. Therefore, TOPD does not necessarily reduce the measured peak GPU memory by exactly ρ\rho, but it substantially lowers the memory associated with long rollouts, especially KV cache and log-probability computation buffers.
